fact: The entire process of building, deploying, using and updating an information system is called the systems development life cycle, or SDLC

The NINE principles of successful systems development are: get the user involved; use a problem-solving approach; establish phases and activities; establish standards for development and documentation; justify systems as capital investments; do not be afraid to cancel or revise scope; divide and conquer; design systems for growth and change; and proper planning and project management
Get the user involved: involving users throughout the process helps ensure requirements are accurate, reduces resistance to change, and increases user acceptance of the final system

Use a problem-solving approach: development should focus on solving real business problems rather than merely applying technology, so developers first understand the problem, evaluate alternatives, then select the option with the greatest benefit and least risk

Establish phases and activities: dividing development into clearly defined phases provides structure and control, making projects easier to manage, monitor and evaluate, and ensuring each step is completed before moving to the next

Establish standards for development and documentation: standards ensure consistency, quality and clarity, and standard methods, tools and documentation formats make systems easier to understand, maintain and enhance over time

Justify systems as capital investments: information systems require significant financial resources and should be evaluated like other capital investments, using cost-benefit analysis to determine whether expected benefits justify the costs and risks

Do not be afraid to cancel or revise scope: if a project becomes too costly, risky, or no longer aligns with organisational goals, revising scope or cancelling entirely can prevent further resource waste
Divide and conquer: breaking a large system into smaller manageable components or subsystems simplifies development and reduces complexity

Design systems for growth and change: systems should be flexible and scalable to accommodate future business expansion, technological advancement and changing requirements, which extends useful life and protects the investment

Proper planning and project management keeps development on schedule, within budget and meeting quality expectations, including realistic timelines, resource allocation, risk management and progress monitoring

A PREDICTIVE approach assumes the development process can be planned and organised in advance and the system developed according to plan, progressing through a fixed sequence of phases with each completed before the next begins; it suits systems that are well understood and well defined

An ADAPTIVE approach is more flexible, assuming the project cannot be planned in full in advance and must be modified as it progresses; it handles changing requirements and uncertainty by developing in short cycles or iterations with continuous user feedback and incremental delivery

In predictive approaches the four activity groups are project planning (planning, organising and scheduling), analysis (understanding the business problem and defining requirements), design (developing program structure and algorithms), and implementation (programming, testing and installing)

Planning, analysis, design and implementation are referred to as PHASES and provide the framework for managing a project; the SUPPORT phase, covering upgrade and maintenance after deployment, is part of the overall SDLC but is not normally considered part of the initial development project
In the adaptive approach activities are repeated in short cycles known as iterations or SPRINTS, each producing a working version of the system or a system component

The adaptive phases are initiation and requirements planning (high-level scope, business problem, objectives, stakeholders and major features, with requirements captured at a high level and prioritised by business value and urgency, often as user stories or feature lists), iterative analysis and design, iterative development or construction, and continuous testing and quality assurance
An example of the adaptive approach is the SPIRAL model

Predictive against adaptive, four rows: requirements defined upfront against requirements evolve over time; linear and structured sequence against iterative and incremental; emphasis on detailed documentation against strong user involvement and collaboration; limited flexibility to accommodate changes against emphasis on working systems over extensive documentation

The chosen approach determines how requirements are gathered, how changes are managed, how risks are controlled and how the system is delivered; selecting the wrong approach can lead to cost overruns, delays, user dissatisfaction and system failure
The SDLC is commonly organised into FIVE major phases: Planning, Analysis, Design, Implementation and Support

The primary objectives of project planning are to identify the scope of the new system, ensure the project is feasible, and develop a schedule, resource plan and budget for the remainder of the project
The five activities in project planning are define the problem (business problem and scope), produce the project schedule, confirm project feasibility, staff the project, and launch the project
Feasibility analysis investigates economic, organisational, technical, resource and schedule feasibility

The primary objective of analysis is to understand and document the business needs and processing requirements of the new system; analysis is essentially a discovery process, and the key words that drive it are DISCOVERY and UNDERSTANDING

The six primary activities of the analysis phase are gather information, define system requirements, prioritise requirements, build a prototype model for discovery of requirements, generate and evaluate alternatives, and review recommendations with management

Information is gathered by observing users as they do their work, interviewing and asking questions of users, reading existing documents about procedures, business rules and job responsibilities, and reviewing existing automated systems
The objective of design is to design the solution system based on the requirements defined and decisions made during analysis

HIGH-LEVEL design consists of developing an architectural structure for the software components, databases, user interface and operating environment, while LOW-LEVEL design entails developing the detailed algorithms and data structures required for software development

The five major design activities are design the application architecture, design and integrate the network, design the user and system interfaces, design and integrate the database, and design and integrate the system controls
The objective of implementation is to produce a reliable, fully functional information system and to ensure all users are trained to use it effectively and efficiently
The five major implementation activities are construct software components, verify and test, convert data, train users and document the system, and install the system

Since the cost of bugs can be immense, testing is one of the most critical steps in implementation, and most organisations spend more time and attention on testing than on writing the programs in the first place
Installation is the process of turning off the old system and turning on the new one

The four conversion approaches are DIRECT CUTOVER, in which the new system immediately replaces the old; PARALLEL conversion, in which both systems run for a month or two until it is clear the new one has no bugs; PHASED conversion, in which small parts of the new system gradually replace small parts of the old; and PILOT conversion, in which a small group of users uses the new system before wider use
One of the most important aspects of conversion is developing a training plan to teach users how to use the new system and help manage the changes it introduces

The objective of support is to keep the system running productively during the years following its initial installation, and the three major support activities are maintain the system, enhance the system, and support the users through a help desk

Maintaining the system covers both fixing errors, known as fixing bugs, and making minor adjustments to processing requirements, while enhancing the system covers major changes driven by government regulations, changes in the business environment, new market opportunities, new competition or new system infrastructure

A help desk is the availability of support staff to assist users with any technical or processing problem associated with an information system; training new users and maintaining current documentation are important elements of this activity
Planning phase deliverables are the project proposal and recommendation, investigation report, analysis of alternatives, cost and benefit analysis, schedule, and recommendation
Analysis phase deliverables are detailed system requirements, revised cost and benefits analysis, and a revised schedule
Design phase deliverables are the logical design, technical design, test plans, revised cost and benefits analysis, and revised schedule
Implementation phase deliverables are system elements, implementation plans, contingency plans, end-user training materials, a maintenance plan, operations plans, and cutover or phase-in
Support phase deliverables are maintenance reports and updated system documentation

Feasibility studies belong particularly to the PLANNING phase and evaluate a project on technical feasibility (availability of technology and skills), economic feasibility (cost-benefit analysis), operational feasibility (user acceptance and organisational impact), legal feasibility (compliance with laws and regulations), and schedule feasibility (ability to finish within the required timeframe)

Feasibility studies reduce risk and prevent wasted resources by identifying constraints early, so management can decide whether to proceed, modify or abandon a project, ensuring only projects with a reasonable chance of success move forward
